intro: The first movement, Allegro con brio, of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5, Op. 67, opens with three Gs falling to E♭, held under a fermata. The movement includes horn calls, quiet exchanges and a passage for unaccompanied oboe, and ends in C minor.

sections.label: A · Three Gs and a fermata
sections.mNote: The opening rhythm passes through the strings.

sections.label: B · Horn call and second theme, violins
sections.mNote: E♭ major; the four-note rhythm continues in the bass.

sections.label: A · Opening motif and horn call repeated
sections.mNote: C minor to E♭ major a second time

sections.label: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
sections.mNote: Short phrases are reduced to single chords.

sections.label: A′ · Opening motif returns, wind added
sections.mNote: An unaccompanied oboe interrupts the return.

sections.label: B′ · Bassoon call and C-major second theme
sections.mNote: The violin melody returns a minor third lower.

sections.label: Coda · High C over a moving bass
sections.mNote: An extended coda in C minor.

cues.title: Opening motif, bars 1–5
cues.text: A quaver rest, three Gs, then E♭ held under a fermata. Three Fs follow and fall to D, which is held for two bars, longer than the E♭. Both held notes come within the first five bars.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts. The second held note occupies two bars.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Horn call, bars 59–62
cues.text: The horns turn the opening rhythm into a broad call: B♭–B♭–B♭, then E♭, F and a lower B♭. The intervals widen, and the music moves to E♭ major.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–62; Mutopia 941, horn part. Written G–G–G–C–D–G for horns in E♭ sounds B♭–B♭–B♭–E♭–F–B♭.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: E♭-major melody, first violins
cues.text: The first violins play an E♭-major melody, marked dolce. Under it, the cellos repeat three short B♭s and a longer E♭. The opening rhythm is now in the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 63–70; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts. Cello figures in bars 65–66 and 69–70.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1808
cues.text: The symphony was first performed at the Theater an der Wien, Vienna, on 22 December 1808. The same programme included the Sixth Symphony, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy.
cues.evidence: Première date, venue and concert programme documented by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: Exposition repeat
cues.text: Two bars of rests, bars 123–124, lead back to bar 1. The whole exposition repeats, with the opening music, the horn call and the E♭-major theme. Each theme is heard a second time before Beethoven begins to break the themes apart.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, repeat enclosing bars 1–124; two bars of rests at 123–124. Mutopia 941 orchestral parts; second performed occurrence of bar 1.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Schindler’s “Fate” anecdote, 1840
cues.text: In 1840, thirteen years after Beethoven’s death, his former secretary Anton Schindler reported that Beethoven had described the opening bars to him with the words “Thus Fate knocks at the door!” Schindler also forged entries in Beethoven’s conversation books, and historians have long doubted his word.
cues.evidence: Anton Schindler, Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven (Münster, 1840), p. 241: “So pocht das Schicksal an die Pforte!” https://archive.org/details/biographievonlud00schi. Schindler’s forged conversation-book entries were exposed by Peter Stadlen, “Schindler’s Beethoven Forgeries”, The Musical Times 118 (July 1977), 549–52; summary in BBC Music Magazine, https://www.classical-music.com/features/composers/beethovens-conversation-books. The motto is also discussed by the Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: Horn call falling to G
cues.text: After the second E♭-major ending, the horns play their call again, this time falling to G. The strings follow with three D♭s falling to C. In this rhythm the strings’ D♭ clashes with the G held by the horns.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–128; Mutopia 941, horns, strings and bassoons. Horn call begins on sounding B♭; strings enter on D♭ in bar 126.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Alternating chords, winds and strings
cues.text: The quick rhythm is reduced to single chords. Winds and strings alternate across rests, getting quieter. The violins move through B♭, C♭ and D♭, then drop to low C♯.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 210–221; Mutopia 941, first violin and wind parts, with diminuendo, sempre più piano and pp.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Oboe Adagio, bar 268
cues.text: The orchestra stops on a chord at bar 268, and the strings rest. One oboe holds its G under a fermata, then descends through F, E♭ and D in a short Adagio. An E♭–D–C–D turn leads to a final D, also under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe part: G fermata, Adagio descent, E♭–D–C–D turn and final D fermata. The strings rest after their chord.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bassoon call, bars 303–310
cues.text: The bassoons play the call that the horns played before. Their G–G–G, C, D, G leads to the violin melody in C major, a minor third lower than before and with different instruments accompanying it.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoons and first violin. Comparison with the horn call and violin melody in bars 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Horn call in the recapitulation
cues.text: In the exposition the horns play the call in E♭ major. In the recapitulation the same call is in C major, and Beethoven gave it to the bassoons, since the E♭ horns would have had to change to C crooks.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, Beethoven site, Symphony No. 5: in the recapitulation Beethoven uses “the milder-toned bassoons” for the horn call rather than ask the E♭ horns to change to C crooks. https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/ Horn and bassoon parts at bars 59–62 and 303–306: Mutopia 941.

cues.title: High C over a moving bass
cues.text: The violins hold and repeat a high C while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F, so the same top note sits in a different chord each time. The coda is long, and more material follows before the final C-minor chords in bars 491–502.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381, first violin and cello; final C-minor chords in bars 491–502. Mutopia 941.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening fermata
cues.text: Near the end, in bars 479–483, the held E♭ of the opening returns under a fermata. Three Fs fall to a long D, as in the first five bars. Beethoven again stops the pulse with the same unequal holds.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 479–483 compared with bars 2–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts: E♭ with fermata, then F–F–F and D tied across two bars.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Silent bar before the horn call
transitions.from: A · Three Gs and a fermata
transitions.to: B · Horn call and second theme, violins
transitions.how: A diminished-seventh chord over C (A–C–E♭–G♭, bar 56) cuts off, and bar 57 is silent. A short B♭-major chord over D follows at bar 58 and points towards E♭ major. The horns then play three B♭s, then E♭, F and B♭ (bars 59–62). Their held note carries into the quiet violin melody, marked dolce.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 56–67; Mutopia 941, strings, oboes, bassoons and horns. Bar 56: A–C–E♭–G♭; bar 57: rests; bar 58: B♭ major over D; bars 59–62: horn call.

transitions.title: Two silent bars before the repeat
transitions.from: B · Horn call and second theme, violins
transitions.to: A · Opening motif and horn call repeated
transitions.how: Three short dominant chords resolve to E♭ major, with the bass moving B♭–E♭ and the first violins D–E♭. Two silent bars follow. The repeat brings back the opening Gs and held E♭, with the strings and clarinets playing in octaves.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 121–124 followed by bars 1–2, second occurrence. Mutopia 941 orchestral parts: cadence, two bars of rests and opening octave line.

transitions.title: D♭ against a held G
transitions.from: A · Opening motif and horn call repeated
transitions.to: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.how: The E♭-major cadence and the two silent bars return. This time the horns play B♭–B♭–B♭ down to G, and the strings follow with D♭–D♭–D♭–C against the held G, so that D♭ and G sound a tritone for a moment. After the fermata, quiet second violins and bassoons bring in F minor over a C in the cellos.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 121–124, second occurrence, and 125–130. Mutopia 941: horn call, D♭–C string response and F–A♭–C harmony in bar 130.

transitions.title: Paired chords reduced to single chords
transitions.from: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.to: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.how: Winds and strings exchange pairs of slow chords. The strings play C seventh over G, then F minor over A♭ (bars 198–199). From bar 209 each group plays only one chord and rests while the other group plays. A diminuendo leads towards pianissimo F♯ minor at bars 215–220. The repeated quavers have disappeared.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 196–220. Mutopia 941 string and wind parts: C7/G and F minor/A♭ at 198–199, single-chord exchanges from 209 and F♯ minor at 215–220.

transitions.title: Diminished-seventh exchanges lead to the recapitulation
transitions.from: Dev · Fragments pass between winds and strings
transitions.to: A′ · Opening motif returns, wind added
transitions.how: From bar 233 to bar 240, quiet winds and strings alternate on B–D–F–A♭, the diminished seventh that points towards C minor. Fortissimo A♭–A♭–A♭–F fragments break into these exchanges and come at shorter intervals. The bass moves from F to three Gs. At bar 248 the opening E♭ returns under its fermata, now reinforced by winds and horns.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 233–253; Mutopia 941 strings, oboes, bassoons and horns. Diminished-seventh exchanges at 233–240, compressed A♭–F figures and return at 248.

transitions.title: Half cadence leading to the oboe cadenza
transitions.from: A′ · Opening motif returns, wind added
transitions.to: A′ · Opening motif returns, wind added
transitions.how: The orchestra reaches G major, a half cadence in C minor. The strings stop, and the oboe is left on G. Its unaccompanied Adagio descends F–E♭–D, turns through E♭–D–C–D and descends again. A fermata holds the final D. The violins then resume with three A♭s falling to F.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 268–270; Mutopia 941, oboe and string parts. The entire Adagio cadenza belongs to bar 268.

transitions.title: Bassoons lead the second theme into C
transitions.from: A′ · Opening motif returns, wind added
transitions.to: B′ · Bassoon call and C-major second theme
transitions.how: A silent bar comes before a G-major chord over B, the dominant of C. The bassoons play the call: G–G–G–C–D–G. Their last G is held beneath the quiet violin melody, which now begins G–C–B–C. The horn call and E♭-major second theme of the exposition return here in C major, a minor third lower.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 301–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and string parts. Compare bars 57–66.

transitions.title: Cadence in C major opens the coda
transitions.from: B′ · Bassoon call and C-major second theme
transitions.to: Coda · High C over a moving bass
transitions.how: G major resolves to C major, with G–C in the bass and B–C in the first violins. The same arrival begins the coda. High C alternates between held notes and tremolo while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F. Beneath the repeated C, the chords change from C major to F minor and back.
transitions.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 373–381; Mutopia 941, first violin, second violin, viola and cello. C major, F minor/A♭, C major/E and F minor occupy successive two-bar spans.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, Mutopia 941, from the Breitkopf & Härtel parts

timeline.note: Clarinets and strings play the opening in octaves, holding E♭ under the fermata.
The strings pass the four-note rhythm upwards above held bassoon notes.
Winds, brass and timpani join the strings for the loud chords and repeated notes.
The strings climb; oboes, clarinets and horns answer their short phrases.
The orchestra plays repeated chords before the pause and the horn call.
The horns play alone: three B♭s, then E♭, F and a lower B♭.
The violins play the E♭-major melody. Clarinets and bassoons answer; flutes and oboes join later.
Falling violin figures lead towards the cadence, with trumpets and timpani reinforcing the chords.
The repeat brings back the opening Gs in clarinets and strings.
The strings pass the rhythm between them again over held bassoons.
Trumpets and timpani rejoin the strings and woodwind for the repeated orchestral outburst.
The rising string phrases are answered by woodwind and horns.
A crescendo fills the orchestra before the horn call’s second appearance.
The horns play alone after the orchestral pause, again moving towards E♭ major.
The violins repeat their melody above repeated notes in the lower strings.
The full orchestra closes the repeated exposition in E♭ major, followed by two silent bars.
Horns and clarinets start the development’s call; the strings answer D♭–D♭–D♭–C.
Quiet strings and bassoons establish F minor; fragments pass through the clarinets and horns.
The horns repeat the short-note rhythm while orchestral chords alternate with string runs.
Wind and brass play pairs of slow chords, and the strings answer them.
The replies are reduced to single chords, passed between winds and strings at pianissimo.
Diminished-seventh chords alternate between groups before the repeated-note rhythm breaks back in.
The opening returns with winds, brass and timpani reinforcing the strings.
Quiet string phrases leave space for the woodwind, and the oboe plays a sustained line.
A G-major chord reaches a fermata; the horns rest.
One oboe plays the unaccompanied Adagio, descending through F, E♭ and D.
The violins restart the repeated A♭s; wind and brass answers follow.
The full orchestra plays up to the pause before the bassoon call.
The bassoons take the call alone: G–G–G–C–D–G.
The violins play in C major, with replies from the woodwind and quiet timpani.
Trumpets and timpani reinforce the returning closing chords.
Violins and upper winds sustain high C while the bass changes C–A♭–E–F.
Fortissimo orchestral chords alternate with the strings’ short figures.
Woodwind and violins play quiet phrases above held notes in the low strings.
The whole orchestra alternates G-major and C-minor chords before the final C.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
